title: Reductive generation from compatible rank-one subgroups
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $H$ be a smooth connected affine $F$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme], and $T\subseteq H$ a split maximal torus, meaning a closed subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for some $r\geq0$, maximal among torus subgroups [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup, def-sc-gm-ga]. Put $X=X^*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathbf G_m)$ and $Y=X_*(T)=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf G_m,T)$, with pairing $\chi\circ\nu(s)=s^{\langle\chi,\nu\rangle}$. Let $D\subset X\setminus\{0\}$ be finite and $\mathbf Z$-linearly independent. For each $\alpha\in D$, suppose given a smooth connected split reductive closed subgroup $J_\alpha\subseteq H$ with maximal torus $T$ and root set $\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$, using the root and reductivity conventions of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Denote its root subgroups by $U_{\pm\alpha}$ [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations] and its coroot by $c_\alpha\in Y$. Assume that for distinct $\alpha,\beta\in D$, $U_{-\alpha}$ and $U_\beta$ commute as subgroup schemes: their commutator morphism is constant at the identity. The smallest closed subgroup $G\subseteq H$ containing $T$ and all the $J_\alpha$ is smooth connected split reductive, has maximal torus $T$, and has simple-root base $D$. Its coroot corresponding to $\alpha\in D$ is $c_\alpha$. More generally, if $J\subseteq G$ is any split reductive closed subgroup having maximal torus $T$ and roots exactly $\pm\gamma$ for a root $\gamma$ of $G$, the coroot of $\gamma$ in $J$ is its coroot in $G$. For $D=\varnothing$, interpret the generated subgroup as $T$. Reductive means that the smooth connected affine group of finite type has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup, with unipotence defined by unipotent geometric matrices in a faithful representation. All assertions concern group schemes in every characteristic, rather than just rational-point groups.

source.place: Theorem 23.31 and Remark 23.33, printed p.494; root-coroot compatibility for embedded rank-one subgroups as in Theorem 21.11, pp.428-429.

proof.text: For $D=\varnothing$, $G=T$. A torus has no nontrivial smooth unipotent subgroup: its points are semisimple in a faithful diagonal representation, so any unipotent point is the identity; smoothness excludes infinitesimal residue. Its adjoint action is trivial, so its roots are empty. Suppose $D\ne\varnothing$. Let $P=\prod_{\alpha\in D}J_\alpha$, with the factors in any fixed order, and $w:P\to H$ their multiplication map. Put $X=P\times P$ and $\varphi(a,b)=w(a)w(b)^{-1}$, pointed at the tuple of identities. Its image is inversion-stable, since swapping $a,b$ inverts $\varphi$, and contains each $J_\alpha$ by taking all other factors equal to $1$. Finite products of these smooth affine groups are smooth directly from the definition: lift maps across a square-zero thickening coordinate by coordinate, and tensor their finite presentations. Smoothness gives geometric reducedness. The generic smooth-connected group assertion gives geometric connectedness of each factor; the product-components lemma, after every field extension and by induction on the number of factors, gives geometric connectedness of $X$. Apply the pointed-map generated-subgroup construction. It gives the smallest closed generated $G$, affine of finite type, geometrically reduced and connected. The geometrically-reduced group theorem makes it smooth. Any torus of $G$ containing $T$ is a torus of $H$, so maximality of $T$ in $H$ gives maximality in $G$.

source.place: Section 2h, Propositions 2.46--2.48; smoothness over a perfect field

proof.text: The perfect character-cocharacter pairing for any one of the given reductive $J_\alpha$ identifies $Y$ with the integer dual of $X$. Independence of $D$ lets us prescribe rational values on it in $X\otimes\mathbf Q$, extend to a rational basis, and clear denominators. Thus choose $\lambda\in Y$ with $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle=n>0$ for every $\alpha$. The same argument gives face cocharacters $\eta_\alpha$ zero on $\alpha$ and a common positive integer on the remaining roots. Apply the contracting-cell lemma to the given $J_\alpha\subseteq G$: the closed-generation, common maximal torus and mixed commutation hypotheses are exactly those of the statement. Obtain $U,V$, the dense open cell $V\times T\times U$, the solvable subgroups $TU,TV$, their intersection $T$, and $U=U_G(\lambda)$, $V=U_G(-\lambda)$, $Z_G(\lambda)=T$.

Apply the simple-root limit-retraction lemma with these cell and contraction identifications. It gives $p_\alpha$, its smooth connected kernel $K_\alpha$, the splitting $U=U_\alpha\ltimes K_\alpha$, the face centralizer $C_U(\eta_\alpha)=U_\alpha$, and extension of every cocharacter nonnegative on $D$ to $U$. Apply the rank-one reflection theorem inside each reductive $J_\alpha$ to choose $n_\alpha\in N_{J_\alpha}(T)(F)$ acting as $x\mapsto x-\langle x,c_\alpha\rangle\alpha$ and sending the weight $α$ to $-α$. Uniqueness of root subgroups in $J_α$ then says that $n_α$ conjugates its two root groups. The retraction lemma says $n_\alpha$ normalizes $K_\alpha$. These are all the inputs required by the triangular-reflection-orbit lemma; apply it to obtain $W,R=WD$, their signed integral simple coefficients, the well-defined subgroups $U_\rho$, and $\dot w_0$ exchanging $U$ and $V$. This constructs an abstract root system without yet asserting reductivity of $G$.

The subgroup-detection lemma now applies: each nontrivial reduced $T$-normalized closed subgroup of $U$ contains some $U_\rho$. Let $A$ be a smooth connected solvable subgroup containing $TV$. If $A\ne TV$, its intersection with the open cell is dense open in $A$ and has point set $V(F)T(F)(A(F)\cap U(F))$. Therefore $A(F)\cap U(F)\ne\{1\}$, for otherwise $TV$ would contain a dense open subset of $A$ and hence all of $A$. The reduction of $A\cap U$ is a nontrivial reduced closed $T$-normalized subgroup. Detection gives $U_\rho\subseteq A$ for some positive $\rho=w\alpha$. The orbit lemma places $U_{-\rho}$ in $V$, hence also in $A$. Thus $A$ contains the conjugate $\dot wJ_\alpha\dot w^{-1}$, since a reductive rank-one group is generated by $T$ and its two root groups. This is impossible: a smooth connected solvable reductive group is a torus, by the unipotent-part/torus-quotient theorem, whereas $J_\alpha$ has nonempty roots. Consequently $TV$ is a Borel. Conjugation by $\dot w_0$ shows $TU$ is a Borel as well.

Let $N$ be any smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup of $G$. It is solvable. Let $N$ act on the nonempty projective scheme $\mathcal B(G)$ of Borel subgroups by conjugation. The solvable fixed-point theorem gives an $N$-fixed rational point. Normality of $N$ implies every $G(F)$-translate of that point is again $N$-fixed. Transitivity on the rational points and the scheme-theoretic stabilizer description then put $N$ in every Borel subgroup, in particular in $TU\cap TV=T$. A smooth unipotent subgroup of a torus is trivial, by the semisimple/unipotent point argument of step 1. Thus $G$ is reductive. The torus $T$ is split and maximal, so this is a split reductive group, as required.

source.place: Theorem 23.31; Theorem 17.9, Section 17f, and the Borel fixed-point theorem

proof.text: We identify the abstract $R$ with the actual roots $\Phi$ of the reductive pair $(G,T)$. Every $U_\rho$ is a conjugate of an embedded root group of some $J_\alpha$, so its nonzero tangent line gives the adjoint weight $\rho$; hence $R\subseteq\Phi$. Conversely take $\chi\in\Phi$. Its canonical root subgroup is $\mathbf G_a$ with conjugation scaling by $\chi$. Its pairing with $\lambda$ cannot be zero, since $Z_G(\lambda)=T$ has only zero adjoint weights. According to its sign, the root group lies in $U_G(\lambda)=U$ or $U_G(-\lambda)=V$. In the positive case apply detection to this reduced root group: it contains some $U_\rho$; equality follows since both are smooth connected one-dimensional closed subgroups. Their conjugation characters agree, so $\chi=\rho\in R$. In the negative case conjugate by $\dot w_0$ and repeat, then conjugate back. Thus $\Phi=R$. Since the orbit lemma gives $D$ as the simple-root base of $R$, it is the simple-root base of $(G,T)$.

Finally let $J\subseteq G$ be split reductive with maximal torus $T$ and roots $\pm\gamma$, where $\gamma\in\Phi$. Its root groups $U^J_{\pm\gamma}$ are smooth connected, normalized by $T$, with tangent spaces the nonzero $\pm\gamma$ weight spaces of $\operatorname{Lie}(J)\subseteq\mathfrak g$. By the rank-one reflection theorem $\dim\mathfrak g_{\pm\gamma}=1$, so these tangent spaces are $\mathfrak g_{\pm\gamma}$, and the uniqueness assertion of the root-subgroup theorem gives $U^J_{\pm\gamma}=U_{\pm\gamma}$. Let $T_\gamma$ be the largest subtorus of $\ker\gamma$ and $G_\gamma=C_G(T_\gamma)$; the rank-one reflection theorem makes it reductive, and it contains the commutative $T$, maximal in $G$ and hence in $G_\gamma$. Since $T_{-\gamma}=T_\gamma$, the unitriangular images under $v_\gamma$ and $v_{-\gamma}$ lie in $G_\gamma$ and are, by uniqueness, $U_\gamma$ and $U_{-\gamma}$. The roots of $(G_\gamma,T)$ are exactly $\pm\gamma$: $T_\gamma$ is central in $G_\gamma$, hence acts trivially on $\operatorname{Lie}(G_\gamma)\subseteq\mathfrak g$, so a root $\chi$ of $G_\gamma$ is a root of $G$ trivial on $T_\gamma$, that is, a character of the one-dimensional torus $T/T_\gamma$; thus $\chi\in\mathbf Q\gamma\cap\Phi=\{\pm\gamma\}$, and both occur. The simple-root generation lemma, applied to $J$ and to $G_\gamma$, each with base $\{\gamma\}$, says each is the smallest closed subgroup containing $T$ and $U_{\pm\gamma}$. Therefore $J=G_\gamma$. As $T$ and $U_{\pm\gamma}$ commute with $T_\gamma$, $C_J(T_\gamma)=J=G_\gamma$, so the rank-one reflection theorem applied to $(J,T)$ and to $(G,T)$ at $\gamma$ uses the same unique nonidentity element of $N_{G_\gamma}(T)(F)/T(F)$; it acts by $x\mapsto x-\langle x,c\rangle\gamma$ both for the coroot $c$ of $\gamma$ in $J$ and for $\gamma^\vee$ in $G$, and uniqueness of the cocharacter with this reflection identity gives $c=\gamma^\vee$. Taking $J=J_\alpha$ proves that its original $c_\alpha$ is the coroot of $\alpha$ in $G$.
